note: Volume I, Number 3, and the most legible issue of the run so far: page 1 columns 1-2 and page 3 columns 5-6 set the advertising cleanly. Five identifications the first two issues could not make land here — the dentist is Dr. J. C. Bradley, the clothing store is Tuthill King's, Frederick Thomas's store is a little west of the bridge and TWO DOORS FROM THE AMERICAN'S OWN OFFICE, C. H. Chapman's third building is a stable, and Newberry & Dole are steamboat agents. It also carries the run's first Marine Journal and a sixty-three name passenger card, which is an arrival manifest and NOT a residents' list.

claims.notes: THE DENTIST FROM THE PREVIOUS ISSUE HAS A NAME: J. C. Bradley. It is the same advertisement — the rest of it, interleaved into line 28 of this same column, repeats 1835-06-13's wording sentence for sentence ('substitution of others, with but little pain', 'badly affected gums', 'office is at the New York House, where [he will re]main until after the Land Sale', 'Ladies visited at their residence, if requested', 'June 14, 1835'). 1835-06-13's claim declined to read the heading 'P | THOMAS' as his name and this is why that was right: the dentist is Bradley and Thomas is the druggist. The business keeps the name it was recorded under so the two printings compile into one entry, and the proprietor is now on it.

THE FIRM'S FORENAME, WHICH THE FIRST ISSUE GOT WRONG. 1835-06-08 line 407 reads 'L. Wilson & Go,' and this signature reads 'INO. WILSON & co.' — Jno., the standard contraction for John, misrecognised there as a bare initial. The gazetteer therefore carries TWO business entries for what is probably one firm, 'L. Wilson & Co.' and 'Jno. Wilson & Co.', and this project does not merge businesses on a reading: the identity policy's merge machinery is for PERSONS and requires a stated rule, and there is no equivalent for firms yet. Recorded here so the next pass can settle it against the page images rather than rediscover it. The trade is carried from the fuller June 8 printing of the same standing card.

claims.notes: THE CLOTHING STORE'S PROPRIETOR IS TUTHILL KING, which 1835-06-08 could see only as the bare word 'TUTHILL' floating in a blob and refused to attribute. The anchor is still short by one word: 'thrve doors north o[f the] at House' — a hotel whose name is destroyed, and this project will not name it, because Chicago in 1835 had several and choosing one would put a storefront three doors from the wrong building. claims.notes: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED PLACEMENT IN THE RUN SO FAR, AND IT PLACES THE NEWSPAPER TOO. 'A little West of the bridge, Water street, two doors from the American office' fixes Frederick Thomas's store against the drawbridge (the previous issue's printing says 'at the Drawbridge' outright) and, in the same sentence, puts the CHICAGO AMERICAN'S OWN OFFICE two doors from it. The ticket asks for the American's imprint as a scene-date fact and this is the only place in three issues that says where the office stood. WHICH WATER STREET IS STILL NOT DECIDED: 'Water street' unqualified, west of the bridge, is consistent with either bank, and the two Water streets face each other across the river. The street is recorded as 'Water Street' exactly as printed, and no bank is chosen. He also leeches and draws teeth, which the run's other dentist advertisement makes worth noticing.

C. M. Reed, and [the su]per[i]n[t]en[dence] of Capt. Thoma[s …] June 19, 1835. [and the sixty-three signatures that follow, each with the place its signer gives as his own]
claims.notes: AN ARRIVAL MANIFEST, AND IT IS NOT A RESIDENTS' LIST — the distinction this claim exists to keep. Sixty-three men who came in on the steamboat Thomas Jefferson from Buffalo sign a card of thanks, and EVERY ONE OF THEM prints the place he calls his own: Albany, Buffalo, Detroit, Green Bay, Saratoga Springs, Liverpool. Exactly one gives Chicago — 'ALP Weters, Chicagn, [l]inais'. So each entity carries its signer's stated home in `associated_places` and nothing here mints a Chicago resident. The epic's first ruling makes a POST-OFFICE letter-list name a resident candidate; a passenger card is the opposite kind of list and must not be read as one. WHAT IT DOES DOCUMENT: a single lake steamer putting sixty-three named men into the town in the week before the June land sale, which is the same movement 1835-06-13's population paragraph describes from the shore. THE NAMES ARE SINGLE-PASS OCR and several are visibly damaged ('4AJ Mend', 'Heary Ki', 'Martin Sct'); `as_printed` keeps every one of them verbatim and the normalized readings correct only character confusions. None should be used to identify a person without the page image.

claims.notes: THE RUN'S FIRST PORT OF CHICAGO COLUMN, covering 1835-06-13 to 06-19 — the week before the land sale and a fortnight before the scene date. Seven arrivals and four clearances in six days: two schooners, a sloop from Milwaukee and a Buffalo steamer inbound, with passengers on nearly every one and LUMBER on the schooner Hiram from Michigan. That last is the useful one — this project builds a town made of sawn lumber and has had no shipping evidence for where it came in. THE CARGO AND DESTINATION COLUMNS ARE CUT down the right-hand edge throughout ('from' with nothing after it, 'for' with nothing after it), so no route is completed that the transcription does not carry, and the June 16 and 'Jude 10' dates disagree in the same paragraph — quoted as printed, with the second bracketed as unreadable rather than harmonised.

Worth recording for what it implies about the building stock: there is property here worth insuring and a market for insuring it, in a town the same paper puts at 2500 to 3000 people. No address, so `none`. The surname is the same as the forwarding house Hubbard & Co. two columns away and NO connection is asserted between them — same surname is not identity, and this project's identity policy says so for persons and has no rule at all for firms.

claims.normalized: [A] MEETING of th[e] i[nh]abitan[t]s of [School District No.] 4 will be held on T[ues]d[ay the …] July, at 6 o'clock P.M. in the P[r]e[sby]t[erian] Church, to take int[o] co[ns]iderati[on] measure[s for] building a school-house [in s]aid district; [the] Election of a Trust[ee], and to [t]ran[s]act [an]y [b]usin[es]s that may th[e]n come before the [meeting]. HYRAM KING, Cl[erk]. Chicago, June 20, 1835.
claims.notes: TWO BUILDINGS IN ONE NOTICE, and they sit on opposite sides of the scene date. THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH EXISTS AND IS USED FOR PUBLIC MEETINGS in June 1835 — a standing building this project can hold. THE SCHOOL-HOUSE DOES NOT: the inhabitants of the district are meeting in July to CONSIDER measures for building one, so at the scene date of 1835-07-01 there is no school-house in district 4 and anything that puts one there is wrong. A negative is a claim, and this is the clearest one the run has produced. The district number reads '&  4' and is taken as 4; the meeting's July date is cut.

That is a plausible yard: a dwelling pair with a stable behind, which is a shape this project's household layer builds and has had no documented instance of. Lath' — Water street, and a book bound in red calf — but that text sits inside the same line as the school-district meeting notice above and cannot be separated from it by any span that stays verbatim, so the quote here carries only the part that stands alone on line 372 and the street is described rather than claimed. Kept for a small reason: a notice that assumes readers walk a named street and might pick something up in it is evidence the street was in ordinary daily use.
